Inquiries of the Ministry a sort of extra latitude in the interpretation of supplementaries as against related questions. When I say "related questions" I mean questions referring to the same topic. A true interpretation of a supplementary question is that it is one which goes to clarify a point which may not have been indicated clearly in the previous answer. I feel that is the true interpretation of a supplementary question. I quite agree that the questions which come forward in what I call the guise of supplementaries may be perfectly proper questions. However, I should prefer to term them related questions. They may be asked, and hon. members have a full right to ask them, but not to have them come in under the guise of supplementaries, as that procedure really in effect usurps the right of another hon. member to ask a question. If we try to work within these ground rules I think we shall see how it comes out.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening just before six o'clock I said I was not impressed with the proposals included in the throne speech for dealing with unemployment in this country. The speech had a tired and musty smell about it. It contained no new ideas. We were not given even a bare outline of the kind of long term measures that are needed to resolve our country's basic problems. In listening to it one might have thought that the government, decimated and discredited though it has been, is still complacent and content with things as they are. Well, they are the minority in this as well as in other things.
When the emergency program to deal with the exchange crisis was announced on June 24 we were told it would be replaced by long term measures of a positive, constructive nature. A month after that emergency austerity program was introduced the Financial Post had this to say about it:
Ottawa, by raising interest rates and cutting down spending, particularly on construction, is demonstrating to the world its intention to revert to policies which governments considered appropriate for the difficulties of the thirties.
Does this help unemployment? Of course not. If there is slower business ahead, as many signs indicate, the present policy of pushing down the brakes instead of the accelerator is clearly one which will need very prompt review.

Some people presumed that the delay in calling parliament was because the government was working out a long term program of a positive kind. Now we find this was not the case. Instead we have been informed in the throne speech that the emergency austerity program will be continued. This is bad news for Canada.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that high tariffs, even when described as tariff surcharges, are not the answer to this country's ills. Cutting back on public works will mean more unemployment this winter. A policy of tight money-high interest rates and restrictive credit-is an abomination that already is causing hardship to many thousands of small businessmen from one end of Canada to the other. This policy also will mean more unemployment this winter than was necessary.
In the short time available to me this morning I shall confine most of my remarks to the harmful effects the tight money policy of this minority government is having and will have in the months ahead. If a complicated piece of machinery is to run well and smoothly, the engineer in charge must see that it is properly lubricated. We know what happens to our own automobiles, even when they are not stolen, if they run short of oil or even if we forget to change to a lighter oil in winter. Similarly, if the Canadian economic machine is to run well there must be an adequate supply of credit. This is the kind of lubrication the Canadian economy needs. If we have a policy of restrictive credit our economic machine will run sluggishly and its gears will grate. It is our fault or rather the fault of the government when this happens.
Despite some of the things the Minister of Trade and Commerce said yesterday, most economists seem to agree that we are at about the peak of the current business cycle, that a downturn in business can be expected some time this fall or in the early months of 1963. Therefore this is the very worst time to be pursuing a policy of tight money. Such a policy is bound to slow the rate of economic growth and to hurry on the next recession.
What we need in Canada these days is an expansionist policy and not restriction. We need ample credit and lower rates of interest. We cannot expect to have lower interest rates in Canada than in the United States. If we did there would be a further flight of capital and more devaluation. But if our rates are high in relation to rates in the United States, and if this is done in an endeavour to entice otherwise reluctant investment funds to Canada, the result in times like these when our own resources are not being used to full capacity will be inadequate economic growth and higher rates of unemployment.

A policy of tight money is, of course, much less onerous for the larger corporations which are usually well financed, and unfortunately far too many of these larger corporations are controlled by non-residents of Canada. There can be no question that a tight money policy tends to accentuate the trend under which so much of Canadian industry has been falling into foreign hands. When credit is restricted our Canadian owned companies find it difficult, if not impossible, to finance and to expand their operations. Frequently the only way out is to sell to some large foreign corporation or to its well financed Canadian subsidiary. I believe we can stop this sell-out of our natural resources and our Canadian companies. We can buy back in the years to come many of the resources and many of the Canadian companies that are now in foreign hands. We can remain an independent country if we want to, but we shall not accomplish these objectives with our present policies.
We cannot get anywhere with a policy of tight money. It is a disastrous policy for Canada. The policy of tight money that is a central part of the government's emergency austerity program is bad for Canada. It is hard on small businessmen and farmers. It will mean more unemployment this winter. It is a policy that will bring misery and unhappiness to thousands of our people. It seems to me that a vote of confidence for this government means a vote for tight money, a vote for high interest rates. I respectfully suggest that members of all parties should think carefully before they cast their votes for such a policy. I submit that a government that favours a policy of this kind should be defeated, and as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker, in his speech on Tuesday the Prime Minister seemed to suggest that he was somehow or other against the policy put forward by the Leader of the Opposition on the grounds that it would cost too much. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if the government does not realize that the larger part of the program put forward by the Leader of the Opposition will be self-liquidating. I wonder if the government does not realize that the cost in terms of human suffering, when thousands of people are unemployed, is something this country cannot afford.
In his speech on Tuesday the Prime Minister attempted to defend himself against the charges of political fraud. According to him the full facts of the exchange crisis were not concealed from the public; the whole thing blew up after the election. Well, Mr. Speaker, what are the facts? In the first four months of 1962 almost $600 million were poured out of the exchange fund in a desperate attempt to defend the Canadian dollar from falling
The Address-Mr. Lewis below 95 cents. This failed. Then, on May 2, the then minister of finance was forced to appeal to the international monetary fund for help for the first time. The terms were stiff. Canada was forced to abandon the floating rate of exchange, something the minister had always refused to do. The rate was fixed at 92.5 cents. In financial circles there were serious doubts that this rate could be held unless we put our financial house in order.
These doubts increased when a senior member of the government announced that he and other members of the cabinet felt the rate should have been put even lower. I do not know, Mr. Speaker, whether ministers realize how sensitive the money markets are to remarks of that kind. Certainly this had a very serious effect on confidence in financial circles. In May the records of the exchange fund were juggled, despite which it became evident that further borrowings had been made from foreign banks. Then in the first two weeks of June there were widespread rumours in financial circles of an impending financial crisis. It is inconceivable, Mr. Speaker, that government officials did not know this. It is inconceivable that the minister of finance and the Prime Minister were not informed. If they were not, who was in charge of the government of Canada at that time?
The Prime Minister's defence seems to boil down to this: "please do not find the government guilty of deceit; instead let us change the charge to gross negligence and incompetence". The defence put forward by the Minister of Justice in his Toronto speech on Monday was slightly different. He seemed to imply some knowledge of the impending financial crisis prior to June 18, but apparently he did not think it was bad enough to justify the unwise course of informing the public, at least until after the election. Mr. Speaker, as one who believes in our parliamentary institution I stand in such awe of parliament that, although I made my first public speech some 35 years ago, I cannot help but feel hesitation as I begin my maiden speech in this house. But I must say immediately, sir,

The Address-Mr. Lewis that my awe was somewhat tarnished as I listened to the speeches made on leaders' day in this debate.
I listened to the Leader of the Opposition and I listened to the right hon. leader of the government, and I felt sad for my country.
I thought of the problems which beset our Canadian people, problems internal and external, problems of human insecurity at home and abroad, problems created by automation which throws men off their jobs at the same time that it promises unprecedented progress, problems arising from a changing pattern of world trade and changing patterns of political and economic power, problems concerning our national unity and the strains put on it by the times in which we live, problems touching the integrity and development of the spiritual and cultural life of Canada, threatened by the onslaught of distorted values sent over the airways by the studios to the south, problems of nuclear destruction, of peace and war, of simple human survival. I thought of all these problems, sir, and I felt desperately sad because the speeches of the leaders in this house overwhelmed and drowned those problems of life and death in a flood of irrelevant banalities and petty political prattle.
I hasten to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that I do not suggest that with regard to human welfare my party is superior to other parties; still less do I claim any personal superiority. No one feels more keenly the immensity of the problems which face us in a world ever on the brink of disaster. What I do take the liberty of saying in this, my first speech in parliament, is that we political spokesmen and our leaders, by the way in which we attack our duties, are ourselves responsible for the cynicism and scepticism of our people about politics, and their feelings of hopeless and helpless desperation. I suggest to you, sir, this is surely the cause of the political apathy about which we all complain. It is the result of the failure of political leadership to show a sense of urgency, or even a sense of purpose, in these overpowering and perilous times.
(Translation):
It is precisely this national purpose which is lacking at this time, Mr. Speaker.
I would be remiss in not saying a few words in the tongue of my French speaking fellow citizens.
As everybody knows, Canada was founded to a great extent by two distinct nations, and our country will come to its fullest expression only if the equality of the French and English languages and cultures is recognized in fact as well as in law throughout the country. It is not always easy to reconcile the two cultures: sometimes they seem to be in conflict.


In the past we were not always successful, far from it, in clearly dividing the purposes of our two main ethnical groups. That lack of success became a threat for the unity and the future of Canada.
In order to correct that situation, our party, at its founding convention, did not hesitate to proclaim its faith in co-operative federalism- the only system that can ensure the harmonious development of Canada as a whole.
With this purpose in mind, we have to seek the means of co-ordinating our economic objectives, as well as our economic resources throughout Canada, without resorting to centralization, and so as to ensure for each province, as well as for the federal government, full respect of their particular rights.
Until now, I think that governments have but rarely taken the trouble to do anything about human distress. Each time they agreed to adopt some social security legislation, they did so because of waning prestige and the realization that it was time to lull the people to sleep again because they were about to wake up.
The people which believed that its needs were being attended to at last, the people which believed in the great Conservative vision, finally realized that visions belong to the realm of dreams.
Therefore, Canadians in all parts of the country have been trying for a number of years to replace by a responsible party the old ones which have both so often and so regularly betrayed the real interests of Canada.
In considering recent developments, I come to the conclusion that no one more than the people of the province of Quebec has so desperately endeavoured to find a new solution. However, such a desperate search should not give rise to false theories or dangerous policies only because they are repeated with a stubbornness akin to demagogy.

The useful theory is the one which claims that modern society cannot really have true economic expansion and security without state intervention, without public investments and democratic planning. To reach such an objective, we must do away with outmoded principles whose application allows the strong to become stronger and tends to make the poor poorer.
The economic planning we are proposing is the only remedy to the persistent evil of unemployment. It will give work to all Canadians and will permit everyone without any exception to enjoy the immense wealth of Canada.

(Text):
In our view, Mr. Speaker, we must have a plan and a national purpose. Much has already been said about the speech from the throne, but I suggest the most appalling thing about it is not merely that it is empty of serious policy but that it shows a smugness and complacency which is as dangerous as it is unjustified. I could respect an administration which admitted frankly that we are in trouble, which outlined frankly the steps it was taking to correct the trouble, and which challenged the opposition to show a better way. But I cannot respect an administration which insists on arguing that everything is well when it is in the very midst of an unemployment crisis, a foreign exchange crisis, an international trade crisis and an economic growth crisis. How many crises does this government have to collect around it before it will admit that things are not quite the ultimate in perfection?
In reality, all the problems and all the difficulties now facing Canada really converge upon one fact, namely that our economy has been proceeding at a snail's pace for some years. It is of course true, and the ministers have pointed this out to the house, that there have been continuing increases in the labour force and, therefore, an increasing number at work. However, this does not answer the problem; it is the cause of it. Our employment difficulties arise precisely because there is a constant increase in the labour force resulting from immigration, resulting from the natural increase in the population and resulting, above all, from the displacement of human hands by increasingly automated machines. Thus the very core of our problem lies in the fact of a growing labour force; it flows from our failure to provide work for all the eager hands looking for jobs.
Similarly, government spokesmen are able to point, and do point, to the fact, that there has been a steady increase in the value of our gross national product in real as well as in current dollars. However, the figure that is much more significant is the one that shows that our per capita gross national product in real terms was less in 1961 than it had been five or six years ago. This is the significant figure, because a nation's wealth must always be related to the number of people enjoying it, or not enjoying it, and in order for a comparison to be meaningful you must eliminate price changes in the calculation of the gross national product.
It is a fact, and no amount of defence can possibly obscure it, that even in the months of June, July and August of this year, even in the last month which was somewhat better than the first two, our unemployed represented more than 4 per cent of the current
The Address-Mr. Lewis work force, and if you adjust the figure for seasonal fluctuations it was more than 6 per cent and almost 7 per cent, at an annual rate. This is serious unemployment by any definition. We accept it now with some complacency because we have become accustomed to average unemployment rates of about 7 per cent and to winter unemployment rates of 10 per cent and 11 per cent.
Our house leader has already drawn to the attention of hon. members a report prepared by a committee appointed by the United States president dealing with the question of unemployment, where they came to the conclusion that Canada had the highest rate in the western world and the United States the second highest.
A precisely similar story is told in terms of our economic growth. The 32nd annual report of the bank for international settlements gives the growth rates of a number of industrial countries; the figures are based on increases in the real product. They show that Canada trailed in 1961 with a growth rate of a measly 1.8 per cent while countries such as Germany, Italy, Norway, Sweden and Finland had growth rates of 6 per cent, 7 per cent, and 8 per cent. Countries such as Austria, France and Denmark showed growth rates of between 4 per cent and 5 per cent. The same thing was true in 1960 and in the preceding three or four years, when the increase in our real gross national product was only about 2 per cent per year. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that these figures cry for an end to smugness and for prompt, energetic and imaginative action.
The astounding fact about all this is that despite the clear outlines of the picture, the government embarked last June, after the election, on a program which is bound to make the situation worse, as has already been pointed out by other speakers. Obviously what our economy requires now is an expansionist program to provide-and I give this as a precise target-an annual rate growth of between 5 per cent and 6 per cent in real dollars. Only in this way shall we be able to provide the 250,000 to 300,000 new jobs which we shall require each year. To do this requires easier money; it requires lower interest rates; it requires increased government investment; it requires increased useful government expenditure and increased activity on all fronts. What our economy requires, in short, if I may summarize our proposals, are:
1.	An imaginative, large scale economic plan developed by the government in consultation with labour and industry and in consultation with the provinces.
2.	A careful but effective direction of investment, private as well as public, into the most productive and most useful channels.



The Address-Mr. Lewis
3.	A massive attack on the problems thrown up by automation to provide for the retraining and reallocation of workers thrown out of work by technological progress.
4.	A generous location of industry program to meet the special needs of the Atlantic provinces and similar areas, and
5.	An easier monetary and fiscal policy which would provide the necessary money, credit and incentives for economic expansion.
This, and this alone, is the program which this country requires.

speechtext:
This, and this alone, is what could save Canada at this moment. An hon. member over there keeps on saying "good". If he persists, I may conclude there is something wrong with it.
Instead, the government persists in continuing a policy of tight money, of reduced expenditures, of chasing the will-o'-the-wisp of a balanced budget while keeping their political fingers crossed. I say, without too much presumption, I hope: what outdated nonsense. A first year economics student could have told them that the more they attempt to curtail expenditures for the meaningless purpose of chasing a balanced budget the more they will slow down the economy, the smaller consequently will be the revenue they collect and the greater will be their deficit. Their policy is therefore inevitably self-defeating. There will be deficits, but they will be deficits by mistake accompanied by a depressed rather than an advancing economy. But I learned long ago that there have always been men in our land who, like the Bourbons, learn nothing and forget nothing.
Demagogues and unimaginative banking interests always confuse government with personal housekeeping, and look upon government deficits as they would on their own personal debts. This, of course, is sheer, elementary nonsense which is exploited demagogically in the jargon of Social Credit and preached puritanically by the high priests of finance who, like so many others, do not themselves practise what they preach. The fact is that planned deficit financing is as essential as it is indispensable in lifting a declining economy to new heights, and in starting a stagnant economy moving. Let me not attempt any theoretical analysis of this statement; let me simply point to some current historical facts.
All of us have been for some years astounded at the economic progress made in various countries in western Europe. We have

had reports about their rate of growth, surprising figures, particularly when we remember that many of these countries had their industries and their economies seriously damaged in the last war and had to rebuild them from scratch, although, of course, with a great deal of assistance, from the United States in particular.
What has been the budgetary situation in these western European countries? France had budget deficits every single year throughout the 1950's; Britain had deficits every year from 1951 to 1961; West Germany had budget deficits in four of the last five years; Italy, from 1950 through 1961 except for one year; Sweden, every year since 1950 except one; Austria throughout the 1950's. The difference between their deficits and ours is that their deficits were planned deficits, deliberately incurred as part of an expansionist economic policy. The result, instead of being ruin, has been a rapid rate of growth, a steady and rapid increase in wages and living standards, and full employment in most of the countries I have named. In fact some of them have actually had a labour shortage, something that Canada has not experienced since the end of the last war.
In short, striving for a balanced budget is sheer madness at a time of heavy unemployment when machinery and plants are standing idle and when our economic growth is almost stationary. Surely it must be obvious that more and not less production is what this country needs at the present time. But the disease has spread. I have noticed in recent speeches by spokesmen for the Liberal party that they too say their goal is a balanced budget. I urge this house to reject this outmoded and harmful proposition at this time.
Thus it is clear that we cannot have much use for the present government. Nor do we. In our view it has persistently shown itself to be incompetent, inefficient, indecisive and fumbling. But let me make clear that we in this corner have equally no use for the Liberal opposition. In our view it has proven itself since its defeat in 1957 to be completely unrepentant. Just before that defeat it had sold an important public utility to American interests and ignored the rights of parliament. There has not been a single suggestion of repentance or of turning away from the arrogance which that party then showed.
We have seen in the last few years, also, that the Liberals have revealed themselves to be thoroughly unreliable. I listened to the leader of the official opposition and to the hon. member for Davenport, who preceded me, refer ecstatically to the need for a health plan

in Canada. The struggle for a health plan in Canada has been carried on by the C.C.F.-New Democratic government in Saskatchewan, and by it alone. It has won that battle in Saskatchewan despite the most cowardly and vicious opposition of the Liberal party, led by Ross Thatcher and supported by one member of this house who sits very close to the hon. member for Davenport.
I remind this house also, Mr. Speaker, of the health program which the Liberal party duly unfolded during the last election campaign. I called it during that campaign, as I call it now, a thorough-going sham and a shameful surrender to vested medical interests. Because what does that health plan offer? It offers free health services for the aged, the pensioners. If I remember the words correctly, and I am sure I do, the plan said they were for some of the aged. It never explained what the word "some" meant. I have always assumed that it meant some kind of means test. It also offers free medical services to young people under the age of 16. The rest of the community between 16 years of age and the old age pensioners, if I remember the words correctly, are to pay substantially less than half of the cost of the medical services; presumably the government would pay substantially more than half. For the worker who earns $3,000 or $4,000 a year, whose family may be the victim of serious illness and who has to pay a medical bill of $1,500 or $2,000, will he really be helped by this program when he is called upon to pay half of that cost?
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, we are driven to the conclusion that the indecent hunger for power shown by the Liberal party in its announcement of a no confidence motion, even before parliament met, was and is thoroughly irresponsible. Indeed, I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that if one was unhappy at the barrenness of the throne speech, one was equally unhappy at the absence of any positive proposals in the speech of the leader of the official opposition. In a speech of more than three hours-some of us timed him-he spent some 18 minutes on positive proposals.

Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned I was referring to the fact that the unplanned boom of 1955, 1956, and 1957 was bound to

The Address-Mr. Lewis be followed by a recession. There was one other thing that happened in those two or three years, and that was that the price of the Canadian dollar went up. For some years our currency was at a premium, with disastrous consequences on our exports. Then finally, as every member of the house and students out of it know, some 18 months ago the government started manipulating the dollar in order to bring its price down; and the more it manipulated, the more it became possible for the speculators to step in and a period of crisis was reached last spring.
I wish to say that the devaluation of the dollar was probably necessary and unavoidable in all the surrounding circumstances. However, in my view there is everything wrong with pegging the rate of the dollar. The most objectionable feature of the pegged or fixed exchange rate is, of course, the fact that the government is forced to pursue a restrictionist domestic policy for the sole purpose of hanging on to a rate; and even that, of course, is becoming increasingly more difficult.
Again I do not wish to go into any theoretical exposition. That is not to say that I understand all about it, but I think I do understand something about it. However, it will be sufficient for me to remind hon. members that the fixed exchange rate today is very much like the old gold standard used to be. Precisely as it was necessary for the countries around the world to get rid of the gold standard because it was restrictive and cribbed and confined them, so it is necessary for Canada today to get rid of the fixed exchange rate. Therefore, to the outline of policies I suggested earlier I add this one, that we must free our exchange rate so that it may itself find the best rate consonant with economic growth and full employment.
A part of the program, of course, must always be concerned with the expansion of our exports; because basically that is the best way in which to meet any of balance of payments and imbalance of trade problems. I have neither the time nor is it for me in our group to deal in detail with the export problem. However, I wish to indicate, as I am about to conclude, some lines I believe Canada should follow. First, I remind the house that there are almost limitless and promising markets in Africa and in Asia, in the new, developing nations of the world. If we had the imagination necessary we would take advantage of those markets through the extension of credits at minimum interest rates for long periods of time. We must apply our minds and our imaginations to the instrument of export subsidies, particularly in the case of our secondary manufacturing industries. We should also apply a great deal of energy and some considerable funds to

research work in order to see whether we cannot find new goods that Canada could produce; I refer to goods which because of their quality production or for some other reason would be suitable to produce for a small market like Canada and would be capable of being sold outside of Canada because of their uniqueness.
Finally, and most important of all, Mr. Speaker, we ought immediately, without any loss of time, start planning for negotiations with the United Kingdom, the United States, the European common market and other members of the commonwealth looking toward free trade between the continents concerned in order to start an expansion of our exports.
All of these things-and this is the basic point of the proposition I have been trying to put to the house, Mr. Speaker-must be part of one co-ordinated and integrated plan. They must be part of one co-ordinated and integrated attack on all our economic problems. Without such co-ordination, one step can easily negative the other. For this reason planning is the essential ingredient of an effective policy.
As the hon. member for Kootenay West, our parliamentary leader, said the other day, "planning" used to be regarded as a disreputable word, a disreputable idea, but now it has become a popular one. In fact it has become so popular that the government and the official opposition vie with each other as to which one of them made a planning proposal first, forgetting to look at history and see where these planning ideas really came from. However, that consideration is unimportant. What is important is that all over the world and in every part of the world economic and social planning has become an idea which people grasp as essential to our modern complex and interdependent society. Reference has already been made in this house to the report of a mission from the national productivity council to six countries in Europe. According to the report, the members came back convinced of the necessity of planning here at home.
I say that only those blinded by outworn prejudices and those who glory in ignorance can any longer suggest that a modern economy can proceed healthily without active and direct intervention, investment and leadership by the government.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that we in the west have very little time to lose. As we sit here debating, crucial events are taking place all across the world. Things have happened in recent days on this continent which make or should make all of us sick at heart, particularly the fact that young students at a

university should act so viciously and should express and show such contempt for the basic moral principles of human dignity and human equality. Events are taking place in Europe, in Africa, in Asia, in America which affect the very future of humanity itself. I suggest to you that so far the battle between communist totalitarianism and our western democracies has not gone entirely well for us. I furthermore suggest to you that the reason it has not gone entirely well for us is that we are too frequently bound and governed by outworn ideas, by inadequate institutions, by agglomerations of greedy power and by outdated policies.
I say to this house, Mr. Speaker, that we must free our western world of these shackles. We must throw them out and we must make democracy a dynamic weapon in the war against poverty, prejudice and ignorance. We must fearlessly and quickly respond to the needs of our own nation and to the anxious demands of a world in revolt against oppression of man by man. Our country, sir, must play a part in this; it should play an important part.
This, as I see it, is the challenge. In my first speech to parliament I hope and pray that we shall have the wisdom and the courage to meet that challenge before it is too late.

This government has been more active than any government in history in the field of housing, slum clearance, urban renewal, aid to municipalities, sewage disposal, building schools, aid to universities and so on. We have had massive expenditures on a scale never before undertaken in this field. This is part of the reason for the deficits we have incurred. I notice also that the hon. member for Davenport is not suggesting we cut down on these expenditures. He is suggesting new ones. In this great book, "Troubled Canada", in which he corrects many of the thoughts he expressed in his original work, he talks about providing 100,000 new jobs through municipal winter works. We have been doing this for four years, Mr. Speaker. I say to him that when he made the statement that it was necessary to provide 100,000 jobs, he was being a piker. Since this program was inaugurated more than $800 million has been spent on municipal works, and some 360,000 jobs have been provided for Canadians.

Commerce when he spoke in this house yesterday will realize that here again this government has led the way. It is also interesting to note what the hon. member for Davenport said in this book about deficit financing. He said:
Deficits are justifiable and may be necessary in periods of heavy unemployment and recession. Some idea of the magnitude of the problem is given by the fact that over the past decade, employment has increased on the average by about 100,000 per year or just about one half the number for whom jobs must be found in each of the next five years.
The decade he was talking about, Mr. Speaker, when employment increased by only 100,000 jobs per year, must have been the golden decade about which the Liberals are always talking and to which the leader of the official opposition referred so feelingly when he spoke. Let me inform you, Mr. Speaker, and the members of this house that at the moment, as a result of policies brought about by this government, we have doubled that rate of expansion in the creation of new jobs. We are doing this now; it is happening now, not two or three years from now. This rate of expansion will be further increased by the measures forecast in the throne speech and to be brought before this parliament at this session.
The speech from the throne placed before parliament a series of measures having as their objective the promotion of this country's economic growth and the creation of new employment for Canadians. The measures are complementary to the measures already brought forward in a previous parliament and which have been effective to the extent that employment in 1962 has been, on the average, consistently higher than in both 1960 and 1961.

In a free and dynamic economy in which people are entitled to change their occupations as they

Mr. Speaker, mine is a constituency which has deeply suffered from the government's unconcern since 1957 as regards agricultural policy. Most farmers back home are dairy producers, and they are facing an unprecedented crisis.
They must invest large amounts of money, first of all to acquire a piece of land, and the equipment they need for the operation of their farms, and to buy the herds which they must improve constantly. Installing adequate cold plants is extremely costly, and today, in order to conform to the requirements of the companies which control milk distribution, they must replace all their former equipment with refrigerated storage facilities referred to as "bulk tanks".
Mr. Speaker, what is in store for the dairy producers as regards marketing?
Our farmers lie at the mercy of the trust shamefully constituted to exploit them to the fullest.
As a matter of fact, the farmers from the economical area of Montreal cannot reach the consumers' market of the metropolis without going through some big dairies, which subject our dairy producers to a sort of unilateral contract called "quota". I say it is a unilateral contract for, according to this agreement, the commitments lie only on the dairy producer's side. He undertakes to supply regularly a certain quantity of first class milk without any interruption or decline, the year round.
On the other hand, the dairy can accept whatever quantity of milk it deems convenient and send the surplus to skimming stations where the producer is paid at the most $2 per hundredweight for milk of the same quality as that which is being sold for whole milk consumption and for which the producer is paid about $5 per hundredweight. This milk is then resold to the consumer at more than $10 per hundredweight, without taking into account the watering down operation to which the dairies-and, as you can imagine, with great pleasure-submit our milk.
You may argue, Mr. Speaker, that the farmer should simply adjust his production in relation to the whole milk consumption market. But, mind you, it is not all that

It is therefore of pressing necessity that the government inquires into this trust and that it takes the required steps to put an end to this shameful exploitation of our dairy producers.

You are no doubt aware, of the value of publicity. Constant repetitions on the radio, the television and in the newspapers, to the effect that some product is the best, unconsciously leads one to believe it in the long run. Well, if this kind of publicity is so good for soap, why would it not be good in the case of milk and its by-products?
We can, through an exhaustive publicity program, create a demand equal to production. Even our Social Credit friends will surely admit that such a plan for free distribution of milk in the schools would be morally good, physically and financially feasible.
I was quite surprised to hear last Friday the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska give credit to his government for the Farm Credit Act.
I believe that this legislation goes back to the 1920's, and that it is due to the Liberal government. On the other hand, it is true that the present government has changed the name of the act and has somewhat altered the lending conditions in 1959.
But if that legislation now finds a certain favour with the farmers of the province of Quebec it is not due to the Conservatives, but rather because the Lesage Liberal government in Quebec enacted a legislation providing for partial reimbursement of the interests charged on those loans by the federal government.
Besides, our friends opposite use that legislation for publicity purposes much more than to really help the farmers.
The fact is that the guarantees asked for in practice are such that most applications are rejected.
The corporation grants loans only to those who need them the least and it asks more in the way of guarantees than any bank would, and that is saying a good deal.
The act becomes too often, with the complicity of certain officials of the Department of Agriculture, a fallacious publicity instrument in favour of our friends opposite.
Let me give you a good example: in the spring of 1962, that is before the June 18 election, a farmer in my constituency approached the then Conservative member concerning a federal loan. The member filled in the necessary application forms and later on sent an inspector to look over the applicant's farm.
Having collected all necessary information, the inspector led the farmer to believe that his chances to get a loan were excellent and that anyway he would hear very soon from the department.
Of course, in the meantime we had the election. In early September our farmer, tired of waiting and wanting to meet his obligations, went to the office of the new Liberal member for his riding to find out about his application. I then wrote to the district inspector and asked him about that application for a loan, and what was the file number.
Do you know, Mr. Speaker, what that inspector answered me? Simply that he remembered that application, for which, however, there was no file number, for the excellent reason that it had not even been considered.

I would not like to give the hon. members the impression that I question the competence and honesty of federal officials. Quite the contrary, I consider that almost all of them are the perfect example of integrity; besides, most of them have been appointed under a Liberal administration.

In the past few days we have been discussing the speech from the throne. It was very enlightening to see the alignment of the Liberal party with the socialist element in the house. When the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) moved an amendment to the amendment today, which clearly means nationalization of industries and control of the lending institutions of the country, the Liberal members applauded. It is very interesting to see just how far they are going in this House of Commons and in the country as 27507-3-141
The Address-Mr. R. M. T. McDonald a whole. I do not think it is in the national interest for the Liberal party to be moving closer and closer to socialism.
With regard to planning, I wonder just what planning was done by the Liberals between 1954 and 1957 with regard to slum clearance, vocational schools and vocational training. The trade deficit between Canada and the United States soared and soared in a period when the Liberals said this country was going through a great expansion. They did not even give any consideration to the influx in population as a result of war babies that was going to take place between 1957 and 1960.
The Liberals talk about the great things they have done. What about expansion of trade? The old, doctrinaire concept is that the Conservative party is the protectionist party and the Liberals are free traders. Just what happened from 1945 to 1957? They did nothing. The tariff structure of this country has not been changed almost from the beginning of Canadian history.
Then they talk about social security, how benevolent they are and what they are going to do. I remember coming here in 1957 and listening to them crying, and saying they were sorry, but that they could give the old people of this country only a $6 increase. Then they went out on the hustings in 1962 and talked about portable pensions and medical and health insurance at the ridiculous cost which they described in my riding. The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), who is a great advocate of free trade only when it does not apply to the automobile industry, did nothing to commend this government for the reduction of the excise tax on automobiles. Indeed, the Prime Minister in his speech proved that the government is doing a great deal to help industry and especially the automobile industry.
In the speech from the throne there are many good proposals that should be given consideration by the house, but the Leader of the Opposition did not want to hear them. Oh, no, he wanted to grab power. The Liberal party was not elected to be the government of Canada. If they had been they would be sitting over here. Therefore it is up to them to look at all the proposals of the government and give them proper consideration. It is very apparent that they are going to support the socialist amendment this evening. I believe this is a great mistake on the part of the Liberal party and I think that the people will judge them on that mistake.
The speech from the throne forecasts expansion, new jobs, increasing trade, a taxation review, increased development through the industrial development bank and portable pensions. Portable pensions are very dear to

The Address-Mr. R. M. T. McDonald my heart as one who comes from an industrial constituency. I have advocated such a move before but I remember that when this was announced in the House of Commons the coleader of the Liberal party, the hon. member for Essex East, questioned the then minister of justice as to why the provinces must give their permission for portable pensions to come into effect. He said we could do it ourselves. Yet the Leader of the Opposition admitted in his speech that the permission of the provinces must be secured for survivor benefits. You can see how the Liberals are repenting all the way down the line for the things they have done in the past.
I should like to refer to the three point program of the Liberal party which really does not contain very much that has not already been started. They talk about urban renewal and providing 75 per cent of the cost. I have been a member of an urban renewal committee in Hamilton for the last two years and it is not a matter of the federal government simply throwing out the money and telling the city of Hamilton or Toronto to rip down houses and throw people out of their homes. There must be a lot of things done before urban renewal can take place. There must be consultation with public and separate school boards and with downtown associations. It is not the prerogative of the Leader of the Opposition to say that the problem will be solved simply by increasing the grants.
He also talked about the industrial development bank and said that the Liberals would do very much more than we have done. By 1956 there had been 349 loans made amounting to $39 million. By the end of 1961, after the Conservative administration had been in power for five years, there were 1,364 loans totalling $71 million. This is proof that the Conservative party has been putting forward these proposals steadily.
He also indicated in his remarks that new nousing for the production of jobs should be promoted by the government. This government put $2 billion into the direct lending market of the country. If his figures are correct that 100,000 jobs are created by $500 million going into the economy, this is proof that the government has provided 400,000 jobs in the housing industry over the period of the last five years.
In the field of education the government has made vocational training grants to municipalities to build vocational training schools, as well as university grants, loans to universities for residences and all the way down the line.
I should like to point out one thing to which I feel the government should give consideration at this time. I believe the time limit in

connection with the sewage disposal legislation and the vocational grants should be extended beyond March 31, 1962 for loans that are presently in effect, so the projects can be completed. Many of the school boards in this country were perhaps a little hesitant about taking up this plan; but most of them, as the Minister of Labour has indicated, have taken advantage of it and some $267 million have been allocated. I feel we should go ahead and permit people to receive contracts in September and complete their contracts beyond March 31, 1962.
I did note that when this vocational program was announced in the House of Commons the C.C.F.-N.D.P. party and some Liberals laughed at it. They said that this was too little, too late. I do not believe $267 million is too little too late. The municipalities, who are very hard pressed in securing real estate taxes to finance school construction, are very happy with the program. Hamilton has a commitment for $8 million and they are very grateful for the government's interest in this proposal.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) expound his proposal for a utopian economy. At the beginning of his speech, he talked about the problems facing this nation. I am sure we are all conscious of these, except the Leader of the Opposition who did not want to discuss them. He just wanted to get the government out without even talking about them. I may point out that the approach of the socialist party is a very sympathetic and easy-going approach. They talk about a system of medical insurance. I do not want to have happen in this country what happened in Saskatchewan. For obvious reasons, I think that there should be a medical plan in this country. However, the royal commission on health services must report. I do not want politicians in this country trying to secure votes merely by saying, "We are going to have a hospital or doctors insurance plan". I do not want them trying to do this merely because they are uncertain about their political future. We must have all the information so that as a responsible government we can do what is best for this country.
The hon. member for York South talked at great length about planning, looking into the crystal ball to see what is going to happen. This was reminiscent of the call of a premier of Saskatchewan in 1944 and 1945. There was talk about abolishing the 2 per cent Liberal sales tax, a free medical insurance plan and government in industry. All the way down the line, everything was going to be great in Saskatchewan. This was the first socialist experiment in Canada and we have found it has failed. Mr. Douglas packed his

bag and left them in a mess. From 1945 to 1962 public debt increased from $120 million to $450 million and in the same period 250,000 people left that province. You look at government in business, nationalization, and competition with free enterprise. You hear Mr. Douglas, in some of his speeches, talk about going into the cement business, the plastic business, the alcohol business and so on. We know this party has gone into a few businesses and every one failed. He did go into the tanning business, the boot business, woollen blankets, and so on, and they lost a million dollars. Then, he went into the printing business, paint business, housing corporations, box factories, brick plant, and so on, and lost another few million dollars. If those in the socialist party who want to plan the whole economy of Canada cannot do this for a little province like Saskatchewan, I think they should be laughed out of this House of Commons.
I can see what is happening to the Liberal party. A man crossed the floor last session. I remember him sitting in this corner over here and telling us about the nationalization of the steel industry, or rather going into competition with the private sector of our economy. It appears as though he has had a great deal of influence on the Liberal party when they applaud so loudly the great socialist plan of this New Democratic party.
During the election and several years before, Mr. Douglas talked a great deal about putting people to work. This is a very important problem in Canada, and we must face up to it seriously. There must be no fooling about it. All during the campaign he talked about getting sticks and stones, picks and shovels and putting these men to work building roads or other things. At the same time, the power commission in Saskatchewan was buying electrical supplies from Switzerland and Italy. I am not saying the Saskatchewan power commission should not go into the competitive market for electrical materials. However, I am saying it is hypocrisy for a man to go across this country and talk about putting people to work with shovels and picks, while at the same time his power commission is buying electrical fixtures abroad that could be produced in my constituency.
Efficiency in government is, I think, a good thing, since it is the biggest business in the country. We have received the report of a study by the Glassco commission and I hope that the government will, without delay, implement some of those proposals. We have spent a lot of money in securing these proposals and I think we should put some of them into effect. At the same time, however, I believe we should set up some machinery for
The Address-Mr. R. M. T. McDonald arbitration with the civil service commission. I do not mean arbitration in perhaps the provincial sense, the way labour relations are set up in the provinces, but some type of committee should be brought into effect so that civil servants across the country can talk to the government and reach a mutually acceptable settlement of their problems.
The next point I would like to mention in my brief speech is the matter of transportation in Canada. This problem has been with us for a long time because of our country's size. There was an item in the throne speech concerning transportation which I think every hon. member should read. It is a worry to me, as a member of parliament, every time the Canadian National estimates come before us and I see the great deficits that we seem to be loading on this country. I have no bone to pick with Mr. Gordon because, in a way, he is a good businessman. However, I feel he is trying to take over the whole transportation industry in Canada. The keynote of the report of the royal commission on transportation is that competition makes good freight rates. From time to time Mr. Gordon has come before the federal committee on railways, air lines and shipping and told us of the many things that company is doing in the country.
I was particularly interested when, in 1959, Mr. Gordon talked about a $5 million item in his estimates for truck operations. These truck operations were to take care of the movement of freight to the railhead in areas where lines had been abandoned. It seems to me, however, that Mr. Gordon is going beyond this type of operation for now he controls running rights from Halifax through to Vancouver by means of long haul truck companies. I do not believe that was intended by this parliament. The royal commission talked about competitive rates being the basis of a free enterprise system. I now feel that Mr. Gordon is going against what he said in the committee. I hope the Minister of Transport will convene this committee as soon as possible so that we may seek clarification of what the president of the C.N.R. is trying to do with transportation in this country. He mentioned a merchandising plan in 1960, under which he could buy trucks to bring loose cargo into the railheads and then transport it across the country by rail. Now we find that with his large trucking firms he is shipping cargo by trucks in direct competition with private trucking firms who, at this time, cannot apply to a royal commission or to the board of transport commissioners for relief, even though the C.N.R. and C.P.R. may cut rates by using the finance subsidy given by the federal government.

The Address-Mr. R. M. T. McDonald
I believe the House of Commons should give serious consideration to this matter and, through the Minister of Transport, we should seek to bring the president of the C.N.R. before a special committee so that we can look into all the ramifications of the problem. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees), has talked about the denationalization of the trucking industry in Britain after the Conservative government came back into power, and said it brought about a great improvement in transportation. Before we give a bureaucrat, or president of a crown corporation, unlimited possibilities to take over rail and truck transportation in Canada, we should thoroughly investigate the matter so that we shall not wake up some morning and find ourselves faced with a greater transportation problem.
The government, under the circumstances it encountered when it came into office in 1957, has done a good job. Of course one can go across the country and point to particular problems. There are always problems, but this is the age of the responsibility of the individual. If people want the government to supply them with jobs and welfare, somebody must pay for that. We must all work together so that we can achieve these things. I do not say the Liberal party did nothing when they were in office, but now they say that under the Conservative party nothing has happened during the past five years. They are very unfair, but I can see what is happening to them. They are moving in with the socialist parties into this new planned economy and the nationalization of industry. That is a most improper thing for a Liberal party which professes to believe in the free enterprise system.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) moving his amendment, and he is a doctrinaire socialist, mentioned that the New Democratic party would direct social capital in Canada; but how can they direct social capital, which in effect means the trust and insurance companies, without controlling them? As a result of what happened with the so-called compulsory medical care insurance plan in Saskatchewan I really do not see how the Liberals, for political expediency, can side with the people who caused that. It was no benevolent thought on the part of the socialist party to advocate free hospitalization and medical care, because it is not free. During the election a medical doctor who opposed me on behalf of the socialist party told the people he could give them hospitalization and medical care for $24 a year. This is hypocrisy. This is bribing the electorate with their own money because the electorate comprise the people who must pay for these services.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to join with those who have spoken before me in complimenting both the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They did a fine job, a wonderful job, particularly in view of what the speech from the throne did not contain, and more particularly with the thought in mind that much of what is in the speech, if the record of the government is any indication, will not be carried out.
I am a new member of the house. I speak with some trepidation; yet representing the second most populous constituency in British Columbia, a riding of which I am very proud, I hope I shall represent it to the best of my ability. It is a riding which encompasses the north shore of north and west Vancouver and runs up the west coast. It includes many industries, mines, pulp mills and factories, and it is the dormitory of many people of varied vocations and high skills who work in Vancouver. They are particularly concerned with trade-overseas trade and trade with the United States-and they want to work with our neighbours as well as to argue with them.
It is an honour, too, to attempt to follow in the footsteps of the Hon. James Sinclair, the former minister of fisheries who represented Coast-Capilano with great distinction for many years in this house. It is a great inspiration for me to be here in a house which has seen many great Canadians do their best for this country, men with a sense of history, a grasp of world affairs and, more important even than that, a confident outward-looking attitude toward the affairs of this nation. It has been a cause of some distress to me to hear the bickering and petty exchanges which have gone on in this house in recent days. More particularly I have become fatigued by the
The Address-Mr. Davis continuing political orations which put party doctrine-words, generally, which are virtually meaningless-before tangible things.
I am responding to the speech from the throne. I want to talk about energy, about power and, more particularly, about the Columbia river treaty. We Canadians have a problem. We live in a changing world. Perhaps that is a cliche. But with respect to energy we now have many choices before us. Fuel oil has become a luxury. Coal is usable in only a few areas. Oil is giving way in many applications to natural gas and hydro power is having to face the challenge of other means of generation. Beyond all this there is the great promise of power from nuclear energy. As I say, people have more choice. Energy is more transportable.
Surely, we should not be concerned about running out of energy. Surely our attitude should not be one of concern about the eventual recovery of electric power. Part of the speech from the throne says that this government will give consideration to the longer term export of electric power. I think this shows a confident attitude which befits Canadians. It is realistic. It is too late in coming, but it is true also of members on this side of the house that they have not yet realized the realities of the technological changes made in our time. We have to be positive and we have to be realistic at the same time. We need safeguards, of course. We must not export something we shall need in the foreseeable future, and we must not give price concessions to people in other countries which are not available to ourselves. However, we shall look after that. We have an energy board to look after it. The setting up of such a board was recommended by the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. It was recommended also by the Borden commission set up by the present government. It was a good idea. The board will safeguard our interests through public hearings at which there will be a full disclosure of all the facts.
We have in this country $6 billion worth of investment in power generation plants and equipment, and the latest information to be published by the dominion bureau of statistics tells us that nearly 25 per cent of that plant is idle the whole year round. Our peak requirements are less than 80 per cent of our plant capacity. We have $1,500 million worth of idle plant. What is the answer of the planners? I am an engineer. I have done some planning. I have even worked for a power utility. The power companies say: if you can get some revenue for your surplus capacity until you can use it yourselves, sell it for what you can get. This is a practical problem faced by utilities not only on this continent

The Address-Mr. Davis but everywhere. Let us spread out our overhead-this tremendous investment. Let us be more efficient by interconnecting with the United States as well as across our provinces. This is the way to become more productive and, incidentally, the way to earn United States dollars. Even if we sell only a fraction of our excess capacity we shall earn tens of millions of dollars of foreign exchange for this country. That is one practical way I see of improving our balance of payments position over the next few years at least.
We are not unique on this continent. We had a little problem some years ago with regard to getting some power back, but conditions were different then; hydro power was the only really efficient low cost way of developing electrical energy. We are reluctantly going to engage in this trade. But what is happening in Europe? There is a cable now in the channel between the United Kingdom and France. The Norwegians, who even more than Canadians are dependent on hydroelectric resources, have taken loans from the government of Sweden to build projects earlier than they would otherwise have been built to produce electric power for export to Sweden. In these developing nations of Europe we find electric power being exchanged relatively freely. We even find an over-all energy program for western Europe. Nevertheless, we on this continent by and large are holding back. We are afraid to trade in power. I say we must trade, we shall trade, and we shall trade intelligently.
I should like to concentrate now on the Columbia river treaty. As a Canadian I regard this treaty with mixed feelings. As a legal document it is superb. Phrased in straightforward language, it takes a complex subject and reduces it to terms most, if not all, of which are understandable to the layman. The engineering data upon which the draft treaty is based is less laudable. New information has been collected since the treaty was negotiated nearly three years ago. Construction cost estimates have been revised and interest rates have risen sharply. Still, it is the over-all economics of the Columbia river treaty about which I am most concerned. As interpreted publicly by the present government it must be characterized as nothing short of a fiasco. It is inconceivable that the government of this country should enter into any agreement, let alone a comprehensive treaty with another country to last at least 50 years, which failed to procure any demonstrable advantage for the people of Canada. It is, unfortunately, another awesome example of this government's continual reign of errors. Had the present government been in contact with the competent utility authorities on the west coast it would have been aware of at least two

things: first, we in British Columbia have many sources of electric power. They are immense and varied. Second, they would have known that energy from various other sources, including coal, oil and gas based power, can be produced at costs comparable to or less than those which can be achieved by repatriating Canada's share of downstream electricity benefits generated as a result of the Columbia river treaty. I am personally satisfied, and this is confirmed by calculations made both by the engineering staff of the B.C. hydro and power authority and by economists for the well known United States agency, Resources for the Future Inc. of Washington, that a combination of fuel burning stations in British Columbia could produce energy at prices competitive with the energy which this government would bring back from the United States.
Most certainly there are combinations of hydro resources and thermal plants which can produce power even more cheaply; hence there is no immediate advantage, in bringing this power back to Canada, certainly in carrying out a program such as that envisaged by this government.
That we have not made a provident deal economically with the United States can be demonstrated in various other ways. In order to build our three treaty storage projects-we are obligated to do this under the treaty-we must put up no less than $350 million. These three dams will cost us at least three times as much as the Americans will have to put up in order to take advantage of that storage. We put up three times as much money as the Americans.
This is no bargain, Mr. Speaker. But there is a complication: we characteristically pay higher interest rates in this country, and under the present austerity program we are paying a good deal more in terms of interest than is normally paid in the United States. As a result of the fact that the projects that we must build cost three times as much in capital investment, and because the interest rates are higher, the power cost to Canada will be between five to six times as much as the cost of the power that the United States will obtain under this treaty. Perhaps our share of his downstream benefit energy will cost us something of the order of 4 mills per kilowatt hour, while the United States will get its share for considerably less than one mill per kilowatt hour. This has all been given in evidence before the congressional committees of the United States. It is public information, but it simply is not information which is known by the majority of the people of this country. No man, no government, no party can be proud of this achievement. If it is not selling Canada down the river, it is

The Address-Mr. Davis selling Canada short. We will never get rich in this way. We will never be able to strike rates in this country which are attractive to industry and which will bring industry here. In effect we are helping our neighbours too much. We are not looking after our own interests in a businesslike way.
This in capsule form is the greatest single indictment I can think of concerning the bureaucratic bungling, lack of liaison in industry, and the high-handed, opinionated action of the government in respect to matters of this kind. We are in a mess, but we have a dire need in this country to put people to work. We must build projects and we certainly need better rates and lower costs in our industries. How do we achieve these and become positive about it? I submit that the only conceivable way in which we Canadians can rescue this treaty in anything like its present form is to sell our share of the downstream benefit energy to the United States. We must sell it or forget the treaty, and we must sell it for a much higher price than the United States is having to put up for its own share of the power. More than that, I believe it should be sufficient to yield us some sort of profit on this public investment in Canada. What we have to do essentially in our sales to the United States, is to earn something of the order of $24 million or $25 million a year. This is equivalent to more than four mills per kilowatt hour. This is the price we have to get in order to break even on those dams, if we are to be forced to build under the treaty. The sum of $30 million a year, if we were to get it from the Americans, would yield us something like five mills per kilowatt hour. I do not know what the right figure is, but it is certainly a substantial one. We must get a price like that if we are to set in train a substantial development in British Columbia which is useful to the people in that part of Canada.
In view of the high interest rates now prevailing in this country, and in view of the objectives of the government's austerity program, it would be a master stroke, I suggest, if we could get the United States authorities to put up all the cash in advance, not just $30 million a year, year after year for several decades, but a lump sum. We have been prepared under the treaty to accept something of the order of $64 million as an all time settlement for flood control. I submit that we should be going to the United States and asking for a lump sum settlement for the delivery of our share of the power over a long term of years. Something in the order of $500 million might be the figure. This figure would give us a profit. It would give us a capital sum over and above the $350 million or $400 million which we have to
put up in order to build these three immense dams. This would be in Canada's interests, would provide us with jobs in building the dams, and would certainly help us to strike rates elsewhere or build projects elsewhere to attract industry. The United States might raise these funds more cheaply than we. By that I mean by lower rates of interest. It would give us a profit in the order of $100 million to $150 million, and we could do great things with this project.
I recommend some such arrangement not only to hon. members in this house, but to those who, I hope, in the not too distant future, will be attempting to negotiate some such arrangement in Washington. This is a crucial negotiation and it is one which must be completed before the Columbia treaty is brought into this house. To ratify the treaty before we know what we can get for our surplus power would be to tie our hands and commit us to hundreds of millions of dollars of investment in terms of controlled water flow out of Canada. Without knowing what price we would get we would be over a barrel, so to speak; we might have to accept perhaps a lower price if we were to ratify the treaty before the actual price was known.
The appropriate procedure as I see it is to get on right away with the negotiation of a price. The term, furthermore, in my opinion should be long enough to give us a good price. Then having a contract for the sale of this energy in our hands, we should promptly bring the treaty before the house. It could then be reviewed at length by our house committee on external affairs with a view to hearing expert opinion and to tidying up some of the details which have been bothering many Canadians for so long. Most notable, in my opinion, is the need to give Canadians the same latitude in respect to the completion of the major treaty projects. At this moment, under the treaty in its present form, we are pinned down as to the precise years in which we complete these three immense projects. The United States can start this project at any time within five years. I suggest that we enjoy similar freedom in respect to our commitments of construction. This is the sort of improvement which I think might well be acceptable to the United States which could conceivably be made in the treaty and made expeditiously. I am optimistic. I believe that it is possible to complete our price and other negotiations in a matter of weeks, at most months. By next spring construction should get under way. But first of all we must rescue the treaty from the hands of those who have been against the export of electric power, and this is why I pressed a question early today with regard to the export of power under the

The Address-Mr. Davis Columbia treaty. I think that this is an intimate relationship, and I do not think, as the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fulton) said, that there is no connection between them. The present government has made its own restriction as to interpretations of how we can trade in energy. They suspect the Americans and even suspect sometimes, I believe, their own colleagues. This is no way to go about getting things done. Certainly it will not put people to work.
The question before this house is one of confidence. Do we have confidence in this government and in its ability to carry out its intentions as outlined in the speech from the throne? It has suddenly, very suddenly, changed its mind about the export of power. This comes as a surprise after all that the Minister of Public Works and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) have been saying about the evils of selling electricity to our neighbours in the United States. The government has negotiated a treaty which, unless we can rescue it by the sale of power at a very high price, will place Canada and Canadians at a serious disadvantage for many years to come. And it has clearly lacked the ability to co-operate with the province of British Columbia and the government of the United States in this connection. How can we be sure that this government has suddenly been transformed, that it is now in a co-operative mood and that it can now reverse the awful economics of the Columbia river treaty, and that it is really prepared to set the stage for a confident, outward looking policy on power. We need action, ability and imagination. This government has made a few gestures. I hope this is more than a gesture from the speech from the throne. However, in view of the government's record, I doubt whether it can follow through. At times I even doubt whether they really wish to follow through. In other words, Mr. Speaker, I have no confidence in this government.
There are two other quite separate matters which I should like to mention. One was raised by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) in his recent speech. He said that during the five years since the present government had been in power the per capita income-that is the income per person-in this country has risen by $65. This is roughly equivalent to $13 a year. May I say that 13 is not a very lucky number. May I also say that $13 should be seen as against an average income in this country of close to $2,000. Therefore, people of Canada, your increase in the last five years has been $13 a year, or about one half of one per cent. Just consider what the reputation would be of the management of a firm which was offering its employees year after year
[Mr. Davis.)
one half of one per cent. This is not a very remarkable performance. It is niggardly in relation to the performance of many other countries. May I say that 2 per cent has been the North American average over the long term and 2 per cent, 3 per cent, 4 per cent and 5 per cent have been typical with most countries in the western world since the end of world war II. This is an accomplishment, but it is not one to boast about. May I say that 13 may be a number that will plague this government for years to come.
I now wish to touch on another topic. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), who is a very well read gentleman, I believe unintentionally misinterpreted a statement which he attributed to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon). It is an objective of this party-I refer to the Liberal party-to achieve a balanced budget. However, it is not the prime objective. The prime objective, as even I as an engineer can understand, is full employment, and with full employment, the maximum possible rate of economic growth. If we do not have unemployment, then a balanced budget is a reasonable thing to achieve; and over the long run let us hope that with good management and, I suggest-with quotation marks around the word "planning"-with good planning, we can some years have surpluses and in other years deficits but in the long run the idea is a balanced budget. I think this is a more correct interpretation of what the hon. member for Davenport had in mind.
