speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this house being composed as it is, I suppose it was inevitable that it would reflect the atmosphere of the recent election campaign. Even so, I find this tragic.

During the election campaign that concluded on June 18, the people of this country faced real and serious issues including those of unemployment, matters concerning security, health, trade, maintaining the peace of the world, issues vital to the continuance of our civilization and of life itself. Yet I think it is fair to characterize the recent election campaign as one in which, for the most part, these real issues were drowned in the sound and fury, the fuss and bother, of a campaign in which the two main leaders seemed to be concerned most of all about their personal electoral success or about their position in Canadian history.
Here in this house the situation is exactly the same. Real issues still confront the Canadian people. Some of the crises that were with us have deepened in the months since the election was held. That fact makes this session of the parliament of Canada one of the most important to be held in the 95 years of our history since confederation. But how did this session get started? First of all, of course, there were the formalities and the ceremonial parts of it. However, when we reach serious debate, what do we get? We get a six hour or seven hour duel, a shocking display, with the two gentlemen who are supposedly the topmost political leaders in this country quarrelling with each other as to which one was telling the truth, as to which one was using the right statistics and as to which one should be in office. You can search the pages of Hansard, Mr. Speaker, for those six hours or seven hours and it is with great difficulty that you will find anything constructive or anything suggesting the seriousness of the times in which we are living. That pattern, I regret to say, is to a large extent continuing. In all fairness, I must say that I think better speeches have been made since leaders' day than were made on that day. However, the pattern continues. We have had it today between the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr). We have the same political partisan fight that is carried on in complete disregard of the fact that these real issues face the people of Canada.
This might not be so bad, Mr. Speaker, if it were only incidental. However, it has been going on for some time. Certainly for the past few years we have had a government that has been directed, so it has seemed to some of us, with an eye to the leader of that government finding his personal place in history. The same pattern has shown itself in parliament to the point where many people wonder whether this institution will serve the purpose for which it was established.
Mr. Speaker, we in this parliament have a tremendous responsibility. This institution,
The Address-Mr. Knowles democracy, freedom, civilization, may well depend upon whether groups of parliamentarians like us, whether we the ordinary members of this house, can take command of the situation and compel the giving of attention to our real problems.
I have already indicated by brief reference what I regard as some of those real problems, and I am free to admit that just about every one that I have mentioned and every one that I have in mind has been referred to time and again by previous speakers. For example, the health or ill health of our economy and the crisis that we face in terms of unemployment have been mentioned repeatedly; but for the most part these subjects become battles of statistics, as the government now in power and the representatives of the last one that was in power each try to prove that one was a little better or a little worse than the other.
I know of no problem facing us, no area where it should be more evident than it is in the case of our economy and unemployment that what we need in our time is a massive attack, a breakthrough, an all-out determination not just slightly to improve the situation but to lick once and for all the problem of unemployment. The Prime Minister the other day drew attention to the statement in the speech from the throne that the government now in power hopes, if it stays there, to provide a million new jobs in the next five years. The Leader of the Opposition in his speech thought he was going one better. I wondered what was coming, only to hear him say that if the Liberals were in power they would provide a million new jobs in the next four years.
We need something a great deal better than that, Mr. Speaker. We need a million new jobs this winter. As a matter of fact, we need something more than just a statistical improvement. We need to order and organize our economy so that the first thing it does, so that its principal aim, is to provide for our people full employment. It is not good enough for governments to put balanced budgets or exchange rates or loyalty to certain doctrines or sacred cows first in the picture. Things like budgets and exchange rates and methods of financing are tools to achieve a more important end. The end is full employment; and I suggest that some day people will read the debates of this house, in fact, the debates of this day, and think it was very sad that hon. members rejected on the floor of the House of Commons the idea of economic planning. They will resent some of the language that was used when they realize that it was by the means of economic planning that economic health was achieved and full employment was provided.

The Address-Mr. Knowles
The plea I make, Mr. Speaker, is that we look at this problem not in terms of just a slight statistical improvement but that we look at it in terms of really conquering it. We are in an age when the word "breakthrough" has meaning for us. We are breaking through in the conquest of space. We are even achieving some breakthroughs on earth itself. We are building super highways, freeways and throughways to try to get the increased number of vehicles on our roads moving. We are, as I say, breaking through in some areas; but here, in the most important area of our life, namely, providing full employment, we are prepared to stop short of it because, first of all, there must be a balanced budget or there must be a fixed exchange rate or there must be no departure from loyalty to the principle of free private enterprise.
What we need in our time, Mr. Speaker, is a massive attack, an all-out program of planning, of spending money on the things that our society needs to increase our social capital, to provide jobs, to provide goods and services for our people. We need to recognize this as the No. 1 job of our society, and if it is the No. 1 job of our society it becomes the No. 1 job of the parliament of Canada.
I say that it is our function as private members in this House of Commons to compel attention to this problem. I welcome the speeches of some private members in all parties who have dealt with it, but in particular we must compel the attention of the leaders of the two major parties in the house to the importance of this problem.
What I have said with regard to a breakthrough being needed in the matter of our economic health and employment is also true with respect to other problems and difficulties that face us. Housing has been mentioned a few times since this debate started, and let us admit that progress has been made in building homes in Canada. But it is still true that there are far too many slums, far too many Canadians of all ages living in conditions which should not be true for human beings. Why? Because of the same adherence to outworn principles that holds us back in providing full employment. Housing is a right. Housing is a social asset that our people should have, that they are entitled to; and if our society, our democracy, is worth its salt we should find ways and means in this parliament to achieve a breakthrough so that within a reasonable period of time all people in this country will be living in good homes.
The same is true in the whole field of social security. I rejoice in the progress that has been made in this field. I rejoice in the progress that has been made since I first came to the house some 20 years ago. In some of those

wartime sessions we used to have difficulty getting the right to speak on the necessity of doing something about raising the old age pension which was then $20 a month payable at age 70 on a means test basis. We have made progress since those days and I congratulate all those who have participated in the making of that progress. But surely the time has come when old age pensions and other forms of security should be predicated, not just on the idea of providing people with enough to keep them alive. Surely the time has come when a country like ours, which can produce a tremendous quantity of goods and services, could provide for people when their working days are over or under any other circumstances a standard of life just as good as they had during their working days.
It is going to take just as much of a breakthrough in the minds of parliamentarians, in the minds of some people around here, to achieve that idea as it took to break through the means test with respect to the old age pension. But this is the sort of thing that is needed, and I plead that we do not take too much time getting amendments to the British North America Act or referring the matter to royal commissions and so on, but that we really go all out to use the resources that are ours for a social security program that gives dignity to the lives of all our people.
In that same vein I mention the matter of health care which was referred to by my colleague, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), in that tremendous speech he made this morning. This is something that our people are entitled to, not just in terms of what they can afford to pay for or what they can afford by mortgaging their entire future, but something they are entitled to as much as they are to elementary education, something that they are entitled to as much as they are to any of the rights, benefits and privileges of living in this great land. But we will not get it so long as there is this constant adherence to worn out cliches and worn out principles that surround the practice of medicine. Surely, it is time for those who practise the great science of medicine, and for those who organize society as a whole, to realize that between them there should be co-operation, so that the full benefits of medical science get through to all our people. I could go on, Mr. Speaker, but the clock is doing the same.
I want to say a word about the international situation. In our time, we must, to repeat the word that I have been using, work for a breakthrough. I agree with those who say if we are going to achieve the peace of the world we have got to exercise the wisest diplomacy we possibly can; we have got to

take a strong stand for general disarmament. But on top of all these things that seem directly related to the questions of war and peace, let us face it: if we are really going to save the peace of the world we have got to raise the living standard of mankind the world around. This, Mr. Speaker, will not wait until the year 2,000. This must come now.
At a time when two thirds of our people in the world are hungry, ill fed, ill clothed, lacking in education and all the things that go to make the dignity of life, we have unemployment in our country and unemployment in the rest of the western world. We have trade problems, and all that. How ridiculous it is, in the face of a world of nearly 2 billion people requiring decent homes, clothing, food, education, medical attention and all the things that we could help to give them if we did a real, all-out job of organizing our economy. This would not only raise the standard of living of our own people but it would operate to raise the living standard of people throughout the world.
It must be obvious, Mr. Speaker, that the key to all of this, the key to our getting started in achieving a breakthrough, is contained in the words of the amendment that this party has placed before the house. Our amendment calls for economic planning, designed to achieve economic growth and to provide full employment. If we do those things we can achieve dignity and a place in the sun for our people. If we do those things we can provide housing, health and security. If we do those things we can play our part in helping to bring about a better world. However, we have to get started on them and not allow ourselves to be held back by these lectures about planning being regimentation, planning being something that is ridiculous, something we do not want. Anyone with any common sense knows that anything that is being achieved in the world today is on the basis of large-scale planning. How did that astronaut get around the world six times yesterday except by the planning of a tremendous number of people? All the things of which we are proud in this day have come about in this way. Yet, we do not seem to have the common sense to apply this concept to the thing that affects us all, namely the organization of the society in which we live. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, we have placed before this house our reasons for expressing our nonconfidence in the government of the day.
We hope, Mr. Speaker, that the members of this house will look at that subamendment, look at the words, and cast their vote on the basis of what those words say. If hon. members are living in the sixties, if hon. members are aware of the problems that face us, if hon.
The Address-Mr. Knowles members are aware of what the future expects of us all, they will realize that they cannot, in conscience, say no to the things we are asking for from this corner of the house.
After the vote on our subamendment is over, we shall come to the vote on the main amendment. As this house knows, that amendment is something that is now in the possession of the house. We will cast our vote on it, not on the basis of the speech that was made introducing it. You can imagine what that would prompt us to do. We will cast our vote, not on the basis of the party introducing it. Their record is too much like that of the party now in power. No, we will cast our vote on that amendment on the basis of what it says.
I believe it is fairly clear from what we have said in our own subamendment, what has been said in the three speeches that have thus far been made from this corner of the house, how much confidence we have in either the government of the day or the party immediately opposite. We think that the time must soon come for the Canadian people to be given a chance once again to make their choice for a program designed to achieve a breakthrough for all our people.
In the few minutes that remain to me, Mr. Speaker, there is perhaps one other thing I should like to say. If we are going to do our job in this parliament we not only have to get down to business and deal with the real problems that face us, but we have to keep this parliament on the rails. I recognize the difficult time you are having, sir, particularly in the first hour of each day, and perhaps I add to your difficulties once in a while. But we will discuss that matter on an appropriate occasion. I agree with you that you, from the chair, have a responsibility to guard the dignity of this house and that we, as private members, have a responsibility to respect the dignity of this parliament, to take advantage of the opportunities that are raised to press our points, but to see to it that the rules are followed.
However, Mr. Speaker, I insist that that responsibility rests in a particular way upon those who sit on the treasury benches, upon the government of the day. On the appropriate occasion I shall have something more extensive to say, and it will be documented and as pointed as I can make it, about a government which in my view, from time to time, flouts the rights of this parliament. In my view the most recent and most serious example of the government ingnoring the rights of parliament was the order in council that was passed on June 24 imposing taxation without due process of law. We have been told in this house that this was done by order in council based on legislative authority and

The Address-Mr. Knowles that legal opinion was obtained that the government had power to do this. This legal opinion was obtained from the Department of Justice. We all know what the Department of Justice is doing when it gives a legal opinion. The Department of Justice is under the government, and too often it gives the government the opinion it wants.
I can get an opinion, too. Lawyers with whom I discussed this matter agree with me that that order in council, to say the best one can for it, is a case of a subterfuge. It is a case of achieving indirectly what cannot be achieved directly. There is in the Customs Tariff Act a section that gives the governor in council the right to transfer goods coming from certain countries from categories having more favourable rates of tariff to those having less favourable rates. But it can be done only by transferring them completely from one category to another, and when transferred to the other category the rate in that other category shall apply. This is what the statute says.
There is another statute, the Financial Administration Act, which gives the government the authority to remit or give back any tax or penalty to individuals where, for various reasons, it is obvious that a tax already paid should be remitted. When one reads that statute, the Financial Administration Act, and the sections I have in mind, it is clear that these are repayments that are allowed. It is a perfectly proper provision, but this government has seen fit to put these two things together and to pass an order in council transferring certain goods to a less favourable rate of duty and then, under the other act, to forgive all of the higher duty that came about in that way, that is, in excess of 5 per cent, 10 per cent or 15 per cent as the case may be.
What has happened here? The government, the executive, legislated an increase in taxation without recourse to parliament, and it does not even have the decency, courtesy or respect for the rights of parliament to bring it before the house for approval.
I did not approve of the taxation by radio that Mr. Abbott gave us in 1947 or 1948, but at least those people later gave the house a chance to enact legislation making it retroactive, and the government of that day had a majority to ensure that it was done. But here a government without a majority proposes to exact taxation without due process of law, and does not give parliament a chance to look at it at all.

It is a decade in which time is giving us a magnificent chance. If we throw it away, it could be our last; but if we in this decade, with determination, do the job we can do, we could build a society worthy of the dreams of centuries. This is a world wide task, Mr. Speaker, but we in Canada have a part in it. Mr. Speaker, like the previous participants in this debate I want to offer you my sincere congratulations. As I am the first Conservative member to speak for the province of Alberta I am sure hon. members will not mind my taking this opportunity to say, speaking on behalf of all the people in the province of Alberta, that they feel highly honoured at the honour you have achieved in becoming Speaker of the House of Commons.
The ancestors of many western Canadians came either from Ontario, the province of Quebec or Europe. Your own ancestors were French Canadians from the province of Quebec, and I am sure your relatives back in that province join in the pride of Alberta that you have been given this high honour.
I would also like to congratulate the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. member for Waterloo South and the seconder, the hon. member for

Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent). I only trust that when I made my maiden speech in the house I did as well as they, and I hope my speech tonight will come up to their standard.
Although I am sorry to see he is not in the house at the present time, I also wish to congratulate another Albertan, the leader of the Social Credit party, who represents the constituency adjoining mine. I recall reading in the Globe and Mail at the time he achieved that office as national leader of that party that he mentioned, or at least he was reported as saying, that he was one of the true Conservatives from Alberta. When he speaks as a Conservative, then I commend his remarks to you, sir.
The last speaker, from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), said he was discouraged because the leaders of the two major parties had hurled reproaches and recriminations at one another. One must look to see where these commenced. I have in my hand the Globe and Mail for Tuesday, October 2, 1962, in which the leader of the Liberal party is quoted under a heading "Pearson Accuses PM of Political Fraud". That has been answered by other Conservative members, in particular by the hon. member for Hamilton South (Mr. McDonald); but when we talk about misrepresentation and fraud I cannot help thinking of the speeches the Liberals made during the election campaign in reference to the devaluation of the dollar. They must know, and we know as Canadians, that when the dollar reached the value it did reach it meant economic welfare for every major industry in the country. When I say that I am thinking of the primary producers, the western farmers, the farmers of Ontario and the manufacturers of dozens of products throughout the country. But when this misrepresentation and fraud was attempted, unfortunately in some cases people had not time to consider it well and they were left with the impression that the government devalued the dollar. The government pegged the price of the dollar. It did not devalue it; and it was complete fraud and misrepresentation on the part of the Liberals when they suggested what it would do to the primary producers of the country.
I am sure that when those same people have an opportunity to reconsider the position, in the next election, they will know where to mark their ballot papers. I am one of those Conservatives who believe there is an old Liberal trick which has been used against Mr. Meighen, Mr. Drew, Mr. Bracken and all other Conservative leaders, with Mr. Diefenbaker being no exception. It is one of their tricks in trade, when in their references
The Address-Mr. Woolliams to the matter of the exchange problem they try to leave the impression that there was fraud.
Now they are launching a new attack on the Prime Minister for his stand at the commonwealth conference and his position so far as Great Britain and the commonwealth are concerned.
Sometimes when we are talking factually it is interesting to go to the authorities on a subject, and in this regard I want to refer to a book, "The Commonwealth and Europe", published by The Economist Intelligence Unit, sponsored by Britain in Europe Limited. It is a book prepared by The Economist with the assistance of over 100 leading companies and economists, not only in the commonwealth but in the United States. It refers to what they have to say so far as the position of the Conservative party is concerned, when they deal with the commonwealth, either economically or politically. But before I quote it I wish to say that, listening to Liberal speakers, it seems to me they have underestimated the problems so far as Great Britain joining the European common market is concerned.
Lord Salter has this to say in the foreword:
Britain's relationship with Western Europe is one of the great political issues of our time. Problems arising from its economic aspects have been given an especial urgency by the formation of the European economic community of the Six and now, in a more acute form, by its decision to accelerate the process of its integration. A new element in the situation was recently introduced by the formation of the European free trade association of the Seven, including Britain. A basis of agreement has not so far been found for a single market covering the whole of Western Europe. Major decisions of policy are involved on both sides, both of a political and an economic nature.
What has been the stand of this party? Why am I a Conservative so far as the commonwealth is concerned? Let us look in this same book to see what these leading economists have to say. Who was responsible for the preference on certain products that come from the commonwealth and are shipped to Britain and vice versa in our trade relations?
I quote again, this time, from page 10:
The origins of the system date back to the beginning of this century when some commonwealth countries began to give preferential tariff treatment to British goods.
So the preference pattern first comes into play in the early 1900's.

speechtext:
In 1919 Britain in turn gave preference to goods imported from the commonwealth and liable to revenue duties, while during the twenties further preferences were granted.

The Address-Mr. Woolliams
But this is what I wish to emphasize:
It was in 1932, with the passing of the import duties act and the negotiation of reciprocal preferences at Ottawa between overseas commonwealth countries as well as between the U.K. and the rest of the commonwealth that the system reached its fullest development.
And who brought about that conference of 1932? None other than the Conservative party of Canada. The Liberals attacked the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) for his part in the London conference of prime ministers. They attacked him for the stand he took in those negotiations. But, surely, when he went to that conference he was speaking for the farmers of western Canada, and for the farmers of eastern Canada in an effort to preserve these preferences which have been built up from their foundation through the efforts of this Conservative party.
It may yet be possible for Britain to join the common market while retaining the system of preferences which this party took so large a part in developing. As a western Canadian I know that we have other industries besides grain. There is, for example, the oil industry, the production of oil and natural gas which has brought prosperity to Alberta, particularly. Nevertheless our primary industry on the prairies is agriculture. This is what I want the Liberals to answer -and I am sorry the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue) is not in his place: what effect would Britain's entry have on the sale of western wheat to the United Kingdom in the absence of the preferences which were built up by this party and this government?
This is what the Economist Intelligence Unit has to say about this on page 95-I would prefer to quote from people who have studied this question, in this case the compilers of this book called "The Commonwealth and Europe".
Three grains, wheat, barley and maize, account for the bulk of world trade in cereals and of two out of the three the commonwealth is a major supplier providing almost two fifths of world exports of wheat and barley . . .
The two leading wheat exporters produce different kinds of grain. Most of Canada's exports, whether grain or flour, are based on high quality high protein wheat which is often combined with domestically produced grain of inferior quality in importing countries to satisfy consumer preference for particular types of bread. So long as this preference persists, Canada has a fairly secure hold on world grain markets.
That is why the Prime Minister spoke up at that conference in London on behalf of Canada. Of course, there is a chain effect attached to this. If the farmers do well, the businessmen in the urban centres and in the cities do well. I know hon. members from the east of Canada appreciate that among the best customers for manufactured goods are the western farmers who buy farm machines.

Combines today cost between $11,000 and $12,000. No one spends his money better than the western farmer when prices are correct and when he receives the proper value of his production. Thus I say that when the Prime Minister spoke out in London in this regard he was speaking for Canada. He was presenting the facts of Canada's case. On a future occasion the right hon. gentleman will be dealing with this subject again, as he himself said. I want merely to place the facts before the house in proper perspective. Again I am sorry that the hon. member for Assini-boia is not in his place. It may be the reason why the Liberals have had to borrow a socialist to explain their policy in western Canada is because of the position they have taken on this and other matters.
What do the people in the grain business have to say about this? What do the elevator companies or the pool operators have to say? They draw attention to the same problem as is pointed out by the authors of the book from which I have been quoting. This is from the Searle Grain Company's report dated September 26, 1962:
With all this, one does get apprehensive that French wheat will flood into the United Kingdom in a volume which, conceivably, could embarrass millers as well as farmers. British millers are not averse to picking up this wheat at a price but we can have too much of it.. .The point is, of course, that had we already joined the common market we would be expected to absorb the French wheat surplus-
This would mean that our exports of grain to Britain would be largely cut off unless we could find other markets.
This is not a new problem. I have heard hon. members from the eastern parts of Canada say: "Not wheat again!" Before my time in this house there were debates on the question of wheat which lasted three or four weeks. The trade in wheat and the disposal of wheat has always presented a problem to every government. If we did not negotiate properly at the table we could lose the largest purchaser of our grain, namely Great Britain. That is what the wheat pools point out.
I listened to what the hon. member for Assiniboia had to say. I shall have to borrow a phrase used by the Prime Minister and describe the speech he made yesterday as a warmed-over version of the speech he used to make when he was with the socialists. I checked, in fact, and found it was almost identical with the one he made in 1957 against the Liberals. Let us take a glance at the agricultural picture when this government took office. We had a surplus of 700 million bushels of wheat, more or less. Wheat was piled up on the farms all over western Canada, in temporary sheds made up of straw, in barns or old houses or even right in the open. Quotas

were at one or two bushels and farmers could not even sell their grain to meet operating expenses. They were even denied cash advances. That was the state of the wheat producers at that time and, of course, when the wheat farmer cannot sell his grain he gets into the production of other commodities such as cattle and hogs. Thus he begins to compete against the rancher. The whole process, as I say, has a chain effect.
Credit can be given to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness), the former minister of agriculture, and in particular to the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton), for their work in disposing of this vast surplus which was built up during the administration of the Liberals. Let us see what some of the newspapers have to say about this.

It will be a good one, no doubt about that. I always choose the best evidence. This is what the Western Producer had to say on April 5: "Wheat board makes record final payment". Again, on April 12, the same paper printed an article with the headline: "Increase in wheat exports seen helping entire nation". The Manitoba Co-Operator printed an article on April 5 saying: "February wheat exports largest since early 20's". Yet despite all this the hon. member for Assiniboia said the export of grain has not been as great over a period of years as it was when the Liberals were in power.
The hon. member for Assiniboia said that the export of grain was not as great over a given period of years as it was during the same period under the Liberals, but he did not say that when he sat in the socialist ranks over in the corner. Mr. Speaker, let us get the facts as far as exports of wheat are concerned. I do not think that the Liberals, especially the hon. member for Assiniboia, would challenge the budget report of the Alberta wheat pool. These figures are taken from the board of grain commissioners. I do not know whether the hon. member for Assiniboia has seen them; he may have got his figures from the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). They seem to have their own dominion bureau of statistics. According to the wheat pool budget-
-Canadian exports of wheat, including flour and bagged seed wheat, totalled 357.8 million bushels in the 1961-62 crop season, according to preliminary figures released by the board of grain commissioners. This represents a gain of about 3.5 million bushels over the previous year.

Now I move on to 1950. In 1950 the Canadian government, having up to that time endeavoured twice to peg the dollar at a fixed value, first at par in terms of the U.S. dollar and later at a 10 per cent discount, found itself, as it thought, unable in the light of the exchange crisis to maintain a pegged rate, and so the dollar was allowed to float free. From October, 1950 until May, 1962 the external value of the Canadian dollar was established in the exchange markets by the interaction of the forces of supply and demand. The decision in 1950 to permit the rate to fluctuate in response to market forces was accepted by the international monetary fund in recognition of Canada's unique circumstances. It was, however, announced that Canada would return to a fixed exchange rate when the circumstances were right. From time to time in the period since 1950 the fund authorities expressed the hope that Canada might find it practicable to rejoin the ranks of those member countries who were in full conformity with Article IV of the fund agreement.
So, Mr. Speaker, we now move on to 1961. In June of that year I announced in my budget that the government considered it appropriate that the external value of the dollar should be reduced to a discount, and if necessary was prepared to use purchases of exchange for the purpose in order to move the Canadian dollar to a significant discount. -that you so drafted your own no-confidence subamendment as to compel the Liberals to support the government?"
"Yes," he replied, "that is so."

He is quoted as saying this would "make it a lot easier, a lot more comfortable for us now to support the government on the more important issues which will be coming before the house".

All members of the opposition were elected for one purpose, and that was in opposition to the government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: A negative approach.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It was negative. No group is here with a majority and, gentlemen, our country bleeds over it. It bleeds because now we need strong government. I watched for two years, and many here watched for longer, when it was necessary to have strong policies, when it was necessary to have boldness and imagination.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: For 22 years.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And this administration, backed by the largest majority in history, more than 200 strong, dared not show that boldness and imagination.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why are you not still the government?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: How can anyone in this chamber, or in the country, expect with reason to see boldness and imagination now when that same government hovers between life and death in every hour of this parliament? This is not a matter of amusement. We were not sent here to collect our indemnities, to live in leisure while the people of the country bleed.

The hon. member for Ville-neuve (Mr. Caouette) has said, according to these clippings, and he appears to have confidence, that the next time the people are called upon to vote, Social Credit will have 140 members. If that is the case what fear can there be if they are prepared tonight to support the amendment?
There was every opportunity for my party's leader, when moving this first amendment, to dress it in all sorts of Liberal phrases to take a small partisan advantage, as did the hon. member for Red Deer to ensure that no one else but the Liberals would support it; and so he might have if he was afraid of dissolution. But we seek dissolution, and why not? We seek it for the obvious reason that the people, since June 24, have not had an opportunity to say what they believe in the words of the Prime Minister and of the Minister of Finance. Do those on the treasury benches seek to have us believe them? Is that important? We are but the representatives of the people in our own constituencies.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

But this evening they have an opportunity to redeem themselves, an opportunity to show to the people who sent them here that what they said up to June 18 they meant, or else how will the member for Red Deer and the other members behind him, go back and explain to their constituents why they are supporting this government. The very thing they went out on the hustings and sought to destroy they are now responsible for upholding.
Mr. Speaker, we ask those members to consider, as we did on Tuesday night of this

The Address-Miss LaMarsh week, the effect of what they will be doing if they do not support this amendment. On Tuesday night they were asked to remove five political words from their amendment. They did not do it. We are asking them tonight to support an amendment which says simply that those who represent almost two-thirds of the people in Canada, having been sent here to express our lack of confidence, do now fulfil our trust and express it by our votes.
If Social Credit seeks to be believed in those constituencies from which it sent members, or in those constituencies from which it hopes to send members, and if it does not show its lack of confidence in the government, then it can never explain its breach of trust with the people who gave it their support on June 18.
We also ask, Mr. Speaker, for the support of those at your far right. We ask for their support and we are prepared to give them ours.

speechtext:
The words they have included deal only with a matter of planning. Well, there are many who might laugh at planning, but no man or woman can plan to marry, plan a family, plan a business, or plan a government without economic planning. It is a part of nature.
This afternoon when the words of the New Democratic party amendment were given to us by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) it was apparent that at least at this time they, like this group, sought to express their want of confidence and did not seek by devious measures to avoid doing that. It surely can be no surprise that those of us on this side of the house are prepared to accept and follow a subamendment which contains the word "planning".
My leader, on January 20, 1961, as he did frequently before that and has done since, as appears on page 1271 of Hansard spoke as follows:
Mr. Speaker, at the luncheon recess, in outlining our own approach as a party to the economic, financial and fiscal problems with which I was dealing, I had emphasized the necessity for planning and for co-operation and consultation between government and other elements in our society. As a central agency for this forward planning and for the consultation which is required in the circumstances of today, instead of the limited and inadequate productivity council which the government proposes to set up, we would set up a national planning commission. We have made this proposal

more than once in this house. Indeed in the last few years it has been put forward in every session from this side of the house, although I think in earlier days we called it a national commission on employment and automation. A commission of this kind would have members drawn from government, labour, management, agriculture and consumers. It would have an expert staff and it would have adequate resources.
This is only one instance of the way in which Liberals in this house in prior sessions have indicated that they feel the need of planning in our national economy. Some members of the Social Credit group have said they would never go along with planning because they do not believe in it. I would ask these members to consider a report which appeared in Le Droit of August 31 last, a declaration of the Roman Catholic bishop of Quebec in which appears these words:
(Translation):
It is socialization that gives a human character to planning required by industrial society.
(Text):
It is obvious that those who lead the church at least believe in planning. All the elements of our society have indicated that there is a belief in planning, and nowhere in this subamendment appears the phrase "socialist planning" as used by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fleming).
I listened with great interest this afternoon to the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis). I found myself in agreement with at least one part of his speech. He believes, as I do, that in order to get our economy moving we should not have austerity but we require, to use his words, easier money, lower interest rates, increased government investment, increased expenditure and activity on all fronts. This is the crux of the matter. This is the one thing on which all the opposition parties have indicated they are in agreement and it is the one thing this government has indicated it will not do.
It is apparent that the hon. member who spoke from the New Democratic party benches was in considerable confusion with respect to the Liberal medical care plan. It is clear from reading a transcript of his remarks that he has not yet read the plan and I would undertake, if he wishes, to send a copy to him at this time. This appears to be the greatest road block in the way of acceptance of the motion which has been proposed by the Leader of the Opposition and I say to the hon. member that if he would read that pamphlet before the vote is taken he would find this road block removed.
I have limited time but I should like to make a last appeal. Perhaps I appeal to those whose minds are already closed-to people who have already made up their minds, false to their trust. But I cannot believe that any man who sits in this chamber has so decided.

I entreat those who have said on every opportunity in the past that they would not support this government to give credence to their words by action and to join this party in voting want of confidence.

In the speech of the Leader of the Opposition, I did recognize the familiar style of the Liberal candidate from whom I won the election in the riding of Quebec East. Indeed, that candidate was and still is known as the personal advisor of the Liberal party.
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that our people do not want to return to the Liberal party.
The riding I represent in this house was the stronghold of the Liberal party for many years. It was even represented by two prime ministers, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, as well as by another great Liberal, the Hon. Ernest Lapointe.
And if I am so proud to speak to the house, this evening, it is because the voters of my county gave me their confidence. It is indeed the victory number one in Canada to have been able to break through that Liberal wall in Quebec East.
The Address-Mr. Beaule
(Text):
Mention has been made of the subamendment moved earlier by the New Democratic party. I cannot say we agree with that. We agree that economic growth is essential to progress. To this end planning is essential. But this does not mean the state planning of the socialists.
Legitimate planning comes directly from the people with guidance from government in the role of referee rather than through government regimentation superimposed from the top. The former is true democratic planning; the latter is socialism. Proper planning encourages freedom and enterprise. State domination restricts freedom, destroys initiative and is maddeningly inefficient. New Democratic party economic planning is synonymous with New Democratic party socialism. That, to us, has been made abundantly clear. We are opposed to socialism and therefore we are opposed to New Democratic party sponsored economic planning.
I might say to our hon. friends on the other side of the house that after their health planification scheme has been forced into the socialist province of Saskatchewan, not a single socialist member was elected in the last election, not even the one who will never occupy the empty seat across. That proves without any doubt that when one has tested planification, one wants to get rid of it.
Socialistic full employment cannot be accomplished without regimentation. We call to witness Dr. Eugene Forsey, Canadian Labour Congress research director and former New Democratic party card holder. Dr. Forsey made this very clear. Support of the New Democratic party full employment plan by Social Credit would imply endorsement of state socialism. We are opposed and shall so vote. Liberal support of the amendment as amended would confirm Liberal inability to frame an amendment indicating their own peculiar brand of socialism. It would constitute an endorsement of former Liberal prime minister King's declaration that socialists were nothing more than Liberals in a hurry and it would, no doubt, reflect the thinking of the present Liberal leader, who was reported as having said in Hamilton that the people should vote Liberal rather than New Democratic party because, as he said, the Liberals could give them anything that the New Democratic party could provide.

And now, Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in submitting to the house another very important issue. If we refer to section 2A of the Canadian Bill of Rights, we read the following: Bill guaranteeing to the Canadian citizens the right to the security of the person which is not endangered today in Canada.

On the other hand, it contains no effective provision for guaranteeing work in the agreements between employers and employees.
The right, for a citizen, to seek a job, the assurance of being able to keep such a job without the assistance or the intervention of a third party, shall also have to be an inalienable right in a free democracy.
We owe Canada a great loyalty, that of the labourer. I believe the time has come when the federal government should take steps to amend the labour code. We do not want to impose constitutions to the labourers, but I feel it is necessary to add provisions to the bill of rights so as to protect the Canadian workers, the men who want to work.
Mr. Speaker, I long for the day when our workers will enjoy the basic freedom of electing themselves their leaders and of seeing to it that they have leaders where leaders are needed. In this regard, I should like to refer to the constitution of the brotherhood of railroad trainmen, where I find, in page 10, the following statement:
(Text):
A non-insurance member is not eligible to serve in any office in the brotherhood which requires membership in the insurance department as a qualification, and further should not be liable for tuberclosis assessments or entitled to benefit in a tuberclosis division.
(Translation):
I wonder whether this is not an indirect means of selling insurance.
At this stage of my comments, Mr. Speaker, I could summarize hundreds of letters from railroad employees in which they criticize their own union.
A railway employee writes me:
As a fellow worker. I should like to draw your attention to the dictatorial trend of the brotherhood, the American union which represents the railway employees and whose only purpose is to get our money by whatever means possible, and especially through compulsory dues.
Here is another letter:
You know that the brotherhood is nothing but an insurance company operating under the guise of a labour union.
Another letter:
We do not enjoy now the same labour conditions as other industries.
And this one:
The time has come for railway employees to take over the control of their organization.
Still another letter:
Needless to describe the control exercised on us all by those labour leaders. When the Liberal party passed the compulsory dues system, it sold us to the American dictators; the Conservative party did not have the courage to repeal that legislation.


That is why I bring all those facts before this house. I sincerely believe that when the time comes for the C.N.R. to sign labour contracts with their employees, they should first choose a really Canadian union.
I also wish to speak on behalf of the many federal employees who have been asking for many years the right to organize and to be recognized as a union by the government.
It is about time the federal government grant federal employees the right to organize and to obtain justice in their demands to the government.
I also wish to tell this house how our youth and our Canadian athletes who represented us at the Empire games have been treated in the past. In previous years, when our Canadian athletes had to represent Canada abroad, it was a real shame to see them begging all over the country the money needed to represent Canada at Empire games and Olympic games. And when those athletes came back home with bronze or silver medals, everybody hastened to congratulate them here in this house.
I know that last year the house voted a substantial amount for the establishment of a permanent commission for amateur sports, but with the austerity program I think the project will be postponed to a later date. However, it is time more than ever for the federal government to appoint a commissioner of amateur sports in this country, but this commissioner should have the knowledge required and be absolutely free from any political link.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that now, in 1962, Canada should at long last belong to Canadians, and the government, following the Social Credit principles, should give our people a balanced economy in order to assure each citizen the standard of living to which he is entitled.
